title: Why You Become Someone Else Around Others
topic: Why People Change Around Different People
hook: Imagine Maya on one ordinary Tuesday.

cast.description: Maya, a young professional, shown in three rooms on one ordinary Tuesday.

promise: The viewer will understand that changing between groups is a built-in way of staying accepted, and learn how to tell a change of style from a change of values.

takeaway.text: When you notice yourself changing around people, ask whether your style is adapting or your values are bending.

claims.text: Maya's Tuesday in three rooms is a made-up example used to show the idea.
claims.role: Gives the viewer a concrete person whose behaviour changes across groups.

claims.text: Sociologist Erving Goffman compared everyday life to a stage, where people present different versions of themselves to different audiences.
claims.role: Gives the concept a name and a respected source: we adapt to our audience.
claims.source: Erving Goffman, The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1956 Edinburgh; 1959 US edition)

claims.text: In 1995, Baumeister and Leary argued that the need to belong is a fundamental human drive.
claims.role: Supports the claim that the adapting is driven by a basic need to be accepted.
claims.source: Baumeister, R. F., & Leary, M. R. (1995). The need to belong. Psychological Bulletin, 117(3), 497-529.

claims.text: For most of human history, being cast out of a group meant danger, so disapproval can feel like a threat.
claims.role: Explains why adapting to others is plausibly built into us. Presented as one explanation, not a proven fact.
claims.source: Evolutionary psychology overview, e.g. Baumeister & Leary (1995) discussion of belonging and survival

claims.text: In Asch's 1950s experiments, many people gave an obviously wrong answer about line lengths to match the group.
claims.role: Shows that group pressure changes behaviour even when the stakes are tiny and the answer is clear.
claims.source: Solomon Asch, 'Studies of independence and conformity' (Psychological Monographs, 1956)

scenes.narration: Imagine Maya on one ordinary Tuesday. Three rooms, three different Mayas. And none of them is a deliberate act.
scenes.visualIdea: Three panels side by side show the same woman in three different postures, as if three people shared one face.
scenes.setting: Screen split in three panels: office meeting, cafe, home kitchen.
scenes.action: Maya appears in each panel in a different posture: upright, leaning back laughing, hands folded.

scenes.narration: At work she's careful and agrees fast. With friends she's loud and sarcastic. At her parents' table she keeps her opinions to herself.
scenes.visualIdea: A quick triptych of Maya: nodding at a meeting table, gesturing wildly at a cafe table, and sitting still at a kitchen table.
scenes.action: Maya in the business outfit nods along, then the scene wipes to a cafe where she talks with her arms up, then to a kitchen where she sits quietly.

scenes.narration: Sociologist Erving Goffman compared daily life to a stage. Each audience gets a slightly different version of you, mostly without any decision.
scenes.visualIdea: The spotlight metaphor: one figure on a stage, with a different silhouette audience in front each time, and her pose changing to match.
scenes.action: Maya stands in a spotlight while three different audience silhouettes appear one after another, and her posture shifts for each.

scenes.narration: Underneath sits the need to belong. In 1995, Baumeister and Leary argued that being accepted is a basic human drive, not a luxury.
scenes.visualIdea: A ring of anonymous figures opens to let one person in. The ring closing is the feeling of belonging.
scenes.action: A circle of silhouettes opens a gap, and a single silhouette steps in and the circle closes around it.

scenes.narration: In the meeting, Maya doubts the plan. Her manager sounds certain, so she says, "Sounds good." At lunch with friends, she takes the plan apart and everyone laughs.
scenes.visualIdea: Two moments back to back: Maya nodding with a held-back thought bubble at the meeting, then the same thought spilling out freely at the cafe.
scenes.action: Maya in the business outfit nods while her manager presents. Then, at a cafe table, she talks with her arms up and the friends laugh.

scenes.narration: At dinner, her father says something she disagrees with. She smiles and passes the salt. She never decided to stay quiet.
scenes.visualIdea: A small thought bubble above Maya holds a tiny crossed-out reply. Her hand passes the salt, and the reply fades away.
scenes.action: Maya sits at a kitchen table, hears her father, smiles, and passes the salt shaker.

scenes.narration: For most of human history, being cast out meant danger, so disapproval feels like a threat. In Asch's 1950s experiments, many people gave an obviously wrong answer to match the group.
scenes.visualIdea: The watching-eye metaphor over one lone figure, next to two clearly different lines with a group of silhouettes all pointing at the shorter one.
scenes.action: A watching eye looms over a single figure. Beside it, a row of lines in a group test where the crowd points to the wrong one.

scenes.narration: We assume one true self sits underneath. But Maya never lied; she let out whichever part the room could accept.
scenes.visualIdea: The iceberg metaphor: above the waterline, one version of Maya. Below it, many other versions, with a different one rising depending on the room.
scenes.action: An iceberg: the small visible tip shows Maya's face, and below the water many other faces wait, one of them lit.

scenes.narration: So is Maya expressing herself, or surviving the room? Maybe both. Next time you shift, ask: did my style adapt, or did my values bend?
scenes.visualIdea: A balance scale with 'tone' on one pan and 'values' on the other, drawn as simple icons, with Maya studying which one is moving.
scenes.action: Maya faces a split path. On one side her tone changes, on the other her values bend, and she looks from one to the other.
